paper_of_week.headline: Human demos teach robots whole-body, environment‑aware manipulation
paper_of_week.summary:
The authors introduce Pixel‑UMI, a framework that captures sensor‑rich human demonstrations and translates them into policies for mobile manipulators with mismatched embodiment. By projecting raw RGB‑D streams into a unified pixel‑wise latent space, the system learns to predict whole‑body joint targets conditioned on the surrounding scene, sidestepping explicit kinematic retargeting. The paper demonstrates that this pixel‑based representation preserves task‑relevant geometry while abstracting away robot‑specific details.

Experiments on a 7‑DoF mobile base with a 6‑DoF arm show that policies trained on 20 minutes of human data can reliably execute pick‑and‑place, drawer opening, and shelf stocking across three unseen environments. Success rates jump from 38 % (baseline imitation) to 81 % (Pixel‑UMI) with comparable sample efficiency, highlighting the benefit of environment‑aware visual grounding.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Leverage pixel‑wise latent conditioning to transfer human demos to heterogeneous robots without hand‑crafted retargeting.

paper.title: Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations
paper.summary: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi

deep_dive.problem: Transferring human manipulation skills to robots is hampered by embodiment gaps and the need for environment‑specific adaptation. Existing imitation pipelines either require precise pose tracking or hand‑crafted retargeting, which do not scale to whole‑body mobile manipulation in cluttered, novel scenes.
deep_dive.approach: Pixel‑UMI records synchronized RGB‑D video, force‑torque, and joint data from a sensorized human operator. A convolutional encoder maps each frame to a dense pixel‑wise latent map that encodes both scene geometry and human hand pose. A transformer‑based policy consumes a short history of these maps and predicts target joint deltas for the robot’s base and arm, using a learned embodiment‑agnostic decoder that maps latent vectors to robot‑specific joint commands. The loss combines behavior cloning on joint targets and a contrastive term that forces the latent space to be invariant to the demonstrator’s limb lengths.
deep_dive.results: On the MobileManip benchmark, Pixel‑UMI achieves 81 % success on unseen test rooms versus 38 % for a vanilla BC baseline and 65 % for a pose‑retargeting method. Sample efficiency improves 2×: the same performance is reached after 10 k demonstration frames instead of 20 k. Ablations show the contrastive latent regularizer contributes +12 % absolute gain, and the transformer history length of 5 frames yields the best trade‑off between latency and accuracy.
deep_dive.limitations: The method assumes a static camera view and relies on high‑quality depth data; performance degrades with occlusions or noisy sensors. The learned decoder is robot‑specific, so transferring to a drastically different platform still requires fine‑tuning. Real‑time inference runs at ~8 Hz on a single GPU, which may be insufficient for high‑speed tasks.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now collect cheap, wearable sensor data from human operators and bootstrap whole‑body mobile manipulation policies without bespoke kinematic models. This opens rapid prototyping of service robots that can adapt to new kitchens, warehouses, or homes by simply recording a few minutes of human work.

one_thing_to_try.action: Record a 5‑minute RGB‑D demo of opening a cabinet and train Pixel‑UMI on a TurtleBot‑Arm.
one_thing_to_try.why: It validates the end‑to‑end pipeline on your own hardware with minimal data.
